name: Arrays & Hashing
tagline: Trade a little memory for O(1) lookups.
core_idea: A hash map (or hash set) trades memory for speed: it turns *have I seen this?*, *how many times?*, and *where is it?* questions from an O(n) scan into an O(1) lookup. Most array problems that feel like they need a nested loop can be flattened to a single pass by remembering what you have already seen in a hash structure.
signals: You keep asking *have I seen this value before?* or counting frequencies.
The brute force is a nested loop comparing every element with every other.
You need grouping (anagrams), de-duplication, or O(1) membership tests.

variations.name: Hash set for membership / dedup
variations.desc: Track what you have seen; `Contains Duplicate`, `Longest Consecutive Sequence`.

variations.name: Hash map for counting
variations.desc: Value to frequency; `Valid Anagram`, `Top K Frequent`, `Group Anagrams`.
code: for (int x : nums) freq[x]++;        // value -> count

variations.name: Complement lookup (one pass)
variations.desc: `Two Sum`: store value to index, then ask for `target - x`.

variations.name: Canonical key
variations.desc: Hash a normalised form: sorted string as the key for `Group Anagrams`, or encode/decode keys.

complexity: Most brute-force O(n^2) scans collapse to O(n) time with O(n) extra space.
pitfalls: Hash maps are average O(1) but worst-case O(n); rarely matters, but know it.
For Two Sum, check for the complement *before* inserting the current value.

name: Two Pointers
tagline: Two indices that collapse a pair search to one pass.
core_idea: Use two indices that move toward (or alongside) each other so each step rules out a whole range of possibilities. On a **sorted** array this turns an O(n^2) pair search into O(n): moving the left pointer only increases the sum, moving the right pointer only decreases it, so you always know which side to move.
signals: The array is sorted (or you can sort it) and you want a pair / triple with some sum.
You compare elements from both ends (palindrome check, container area).
You filter or partition in place (move zeroes, remove duplicates).

variations.name: Opposite ends (converging)
variations.desc: `Two Sum II`, `Container With Most Water`, `Valid Palindrome`.
code: if (sum < target) L++;   // need bigger -> raise the low end
else              R--;   // need smaller -> lower the high end

variations.name: Fast & slow (same direction)
variations.desc: A write pointer trails a read pointer; in-place dedup, move zeroes.

variations.name: Anchor + inner two pointers
variations.desc: Fix one index, two-pointer the rest: `3Sum` / `4Sum` run an O(n) sweep inside an O(n) loop = O(n^2).

complexity: O(n) for a single sweep, O(n log n) when a sort is needed first; O(1) extra space.
pitfalls: Skip duplicates correctly in 3Sum (advance L / R past equal values).
Mind the boundary: `L < R` vs `L <= R` changes which pairs you visit.

name: Sliding Window
tagline: A moving range over contiguous data.
core_idea: Maintain a contiguous window `[L, R]` over an array or string and slide it instead of re-scanning. Expand `R` to include new elements; when the window breaks a constraint, shrink from `L`. Each element enters and leaves the window once, so an O(n^2) *check every subarray* becomes O(n).
signals: *Longest / shortest / max / min* contiguous subarray or substring satisfying a rule.
Constraints like *at most K distinct*, *sum >= target*, *no repeating characters*.

variations.name: Fixed-size window
variations.desc: `L` and `R` move in lockstep; max sum of k consecutive, rolling averages.
code: if (R >= k) sum -= a[R - k];        // drop the element leaving

variations.name: Variable-size window
variations.desc: Grow `R`; shrink `L` while the constraint is violated; record the best valid window.
code: while (cnt[s[R]] > 1) cnt[s[L++]]--;   // shrink until no repeat

variations.name: Window + frequency map
variations.desc: Track counts inside the window: `Minimum Window Substring`, `Permutation in String`.

complexity: O(n) time (each index is visited by L and R at most once), O(k) or O(alphabet) space.
pitfalls: Update the answer at the right moment: any valid state for *maximum*, after shrinking for *minimum*.
Remove the outgoing element's contribution when `L` advances.

name: Prefix Sum
tagline: Precompute totals; answer any range in O(1).
core_idea: Precompute cumulative totals so any range query becomes one subtraction. With `prefix[i] = a[0] + ... + a[i-1]`, the sum of range `[i, j)` is `prefix[j] - prefix[i]` in O(1). Pair it with a hash map to *count* subarrays whose sum hits a target.
signals: Many range-sum / range-aggregate queries over a static array.
*Number of subarrays summing to K*, subarray with a given sum, equal partitions.
2D version: repeated submatrix sums.

variations.name: 1D prefix array
variations.desc: Instant range sums after O(n) preprocessing.
code: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i];

variations.name: Prefix + hash map (count = K)
variations.desc: Store how often each prefix value occurred; count subarrays summing to k.
code: ans += seen[sum - k];      // prefixes that close a K-sum window

variations.name: 2D prefix sum
variations.desc: Inclusion-exclusion for submatrix sums (`Range Sum Query 2D`).

variations.name: Difference array
variations.desc: The inverse trick: apply many range updates in O(1) each, then one pass to materialise.

complexity: O(n) build, O(1) per query; the hash-map counting variant is O(n) total.
pitfalls: Keep one convention for inclusive vs exclusive bounds to avoid off-by-one bugs.
Seed the map with `{0: 1}` so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.

name: Binary Search
tagline: Halve a monotonic search space each step.
core_idea: Repeatedly halve a search space using a yes/no test that is **monotonic** (once it flips from no to yes it never flips back). Classic on sorted arrays, but the real power is *binary search on the answer*: guess a candidate value, check feasibility, discard half the range — turning O(n) or O(n^2) searches into O(log n) or O(n log n).
signals: Sorted (or rotated-sorted) input and you are locating a value or a boundary.
*Minimum / maximum X such that condition(X) holds* with a monotonic condition.
The answer lives in a numeric range you can test feasibility against (min capacity, Koko eating bananas).

variations.name: Classic search
variations.desc: Find a target's index in a sorted array.

variations.name: Lower / upper bound
variations.desc: Leftmost index >= target, rightmost, or the count of a value (boundary search).

variations.name: Binary search on the answer
variations.desc: Guess a value, test feasibility, shrink the range toward the smallest that works.
code: if (feasible(mid)) hi = mid;        // works -> try smaller
else               lo = mid + 1;   // too small -> go bigger

variations.name: Rotated / 2D
variations.desc: `Search in Rotated Sorted Array`, searching a row-and-column sorted matrix.

complexity: O(log n) per search; binary-search-on-answer is O(n log(range)).
pitfalls: Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` to avoid integer overflow.
Match the invariant (`lo <= hi` vs `lo < hi`) and make sure the range shrinks every step.

name: Stack & Monotonic Stack
tagline: LIFO memory for nesting and next-greater.
core_idea: A stack (LIFO) remembers *the most recent unresolved thing*, which is exactly what nested / matching problems need. A **monotonic stack** keeps its elements sorted; when a new element breaks the order it pops the violators — and each pop is the moment you have found that element's *next greater / smaller* neighbour, in O(1) amortised.
signals: Matching or nesting: parentheses, expression evaluation, path simplification.
*Next greater element*, *previous smaller*, daily temperatures, stock span.
Histogram / rectangle areas, trapping rain water.

variations.name: Plain stack (matching & parsing)
variations.desc: `Valid Parentheses`, evaluate reverse-Polish, simplify a path.

variations.name: Monotonic stack (next greater)
variations.desc: Store indices; pop while the incoming value dominates the top.

variations.name: Monotonic stack for areas
variations.desc: `Largest Rectangle in Histogram`, `Trapping Rain Water` — widths come from popped indices.

complexity: O(n) — each element is pushed and popped at most once.
pitfalls: Decide whether to store values or indices (area problems need indices for widths).
Pick increasing vs decreasing depending on next-greater vs next-smaller.

name: Linked Lists
tagline: Pointer surgery: dummy heads and fast/slow.
core_idea: A linked list is a chain of nodes joined by pointers; you cannot index into it, so almost every trick is careful manipulation of `next`. Two ideas unlock most problems: the **fast/slow** two-pointer (middle, cycle, nth-from-end) and a **dummy head** node (so insert/delete at the front needs no special case).
signals: In-place reversal, merging sorted lists, reordering nodes.
*Find the middle / detect a cycle / remove nth from end* without knowing the length.
You add or remove nodes and want to avoid special-casing the head.

variations.name: Dummy node + rewiring
variations.desc: Merge two sorted lists, remove elements, partition.
code: if (a->val <= b->val) { tail->next = a; a = a->next; }

variations.name: Iterative reversal
variations.desc: Flip `next` pointers with a three-pointer dance.

variations.name: Fast & slow pointers
variations.desc: Middle node, Floyd cycle detection, nth-from-end — slow moves 1, fast moves 2.

complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space for most pointer manipulations.
pitfalls: Losing the rest of the list — save `next` before you overwrite it.
Forgetting to null-terminate the tail, creating an accidental cycle.

name: Trees
tagline: Recurse on subtrees; pick your traversal.
core_idea: A binary tree is a recursive structure — each node owns two smaller trees — so the natural tool is **recursion / DFS**: solve the children, then combine. The traversal order (preorder / inorder / postorder) or level-order **BFS** decides *when* you visit each node, and that choice is usually the whole solution.
signals: Anything over a tree: depth, balance, path sums, lowest common ancestor.
*Per level* questions point to BFS; *combine results from subtrees* points to postorder DFS.
Serialize / deserialize, or build a tree from its traversals.

variations.name: DFS recursion (divide & combine)
variations.desc: Height, diameter, path sum, LCA — solve children, merge upward.

variations.name: BFS / level-order (queue)
variations.desc: Level averages, right-side view, minimum depth — process one full level at a time.
code: int sz = q.size();                    // one whole level

variations.name: Traversal orders
variations.desc: Inorder (sorted for a BST), preorder (clone / serialize), postorder (delete / aggregate).

complexity: O(n) to visit every node; recursion stack is O(h), the height (h can be n when skewed).
pitfalls: Always handle the null-node base case.
Return multiple facts from one DFS (e.g. height *and* is-balanced) to stay O(n).

name: Binary Search Tree (BST)
tagline: An ordered tree: go left or right to search.
core_idea: A BST keeps a global order: every node's left subtree is smaller and its right subtree is larger. That invariant turns search, insert, and delete into a guided walk — at each node you go left or right, halving the work — and an **inorder traversal** emits the values fully sorted.
signals: Sorted-order operations on a dynamic set: insert / delete / lookup, kth smallest, range queries.
*Validate BST*, *inorder successor*, *convert sorted array to BST*.

variations.name: Ordered search / insert
variations.desc: Exploit the invariant to descend exactly one side.

variations.name: Inorder = sorted sequence
variations.desc: Validate a BST, find the kth smallest, or do two-sum within a BST.

variations.name: Range / bounds checking
variations.desc: Pass `(low, high)` limits down to validate the whole subtree.
code: bool valid(TreeNode* r, long lo, long hi) {
if (r->val <= lo || r->val >= hi) return false;
return valid(r->left, lo, r->val) && valid(r->right, r->val, hi);

complexity: O(h) per operation — O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if degenerate; self-balancing trees guarantee O(log n).
pitfalls: An unbalanced BST degrades to a linked list — mention AVL / Red-Black variants.
Use strict bounds when validating so equal values are rejected.

name: Tries
tagline: Share prefixes; query in O(word length).
core_idea: A trie (prefix tree) stores strings by sharing common prefixes along a path of nodes, one character per edge. Lookups and prefix queries cost O(L) in the length of the word — independent of how many words are stored — which is why tries power autocomplete, spell-check, and word-search puzzles.
signals: Many strings sharing prefixes; *starts with*, autocomplete, dictionary lookups.
Word-search / board problems where you prune branches by prefix.
Bitwise tries for maximum-XOR-pair problems.

complexity: O(L) per insert / search where L is the word length; space O(total characters x alphabet).
pitfalls: Arrays of 26+ children waste memory; a hash map of children is leaner for sparse alphabets.
Mark word ends explicitly so prefixes are not mistaken for complete words.

name: Heaps / Priority Queue
tagline: Always pull the current best in O(log n).
core_idea: A heap is a binary tree kept in an array that always hands you the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) element in O(1), with O(log n) insert and pop. Reach for it whenever you repeatedly need *the current best* from a changing set — top-K, merging streams, scheduling — without paying to fully sort.
signals: *Top K*, *K largest / smallest / closest*, *Kth largest*.
Merge K sorted lists or streams; running median (two heaps).
Greedy scheduling where you always grab the current min / max (Dijkstra, task scheduler).

variations.name: Top-K with a size-K heap
variations.desc: Keep a min-heap of size K; its top is the Kth largest.
code: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> minHeap;  // smallest on top
if (minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.pop();   // drop the smallest
// minHeap now holds the K largest values

variations.name: Merge K sorted lists
variations.desc: Push every list head, pop the minimum, push that node's successor.

variations.name: Two heaps (running median)
variations.desc: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced.

complexity: push / pop O(log n), peek O(1); top-K is O(n log k).
pitfalls: C++ `priority_queue` is a max-heap by default — use `greater<>` for a min-heap.
For *K largest* keep a min-heap of size K, not a max-heap of everything.

name: Graphs — BFS / DFS
tagline: Explore everything reachable.
core_idea: A graph is nodes joined by edges; most basic graph questions are *explore everything reachable* via BFS or DFS. **BFS** (a queue) explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; **DFS** (recursion or a stack) dives deep and is natural for connectivity, cycles, and ordering. A grid is just a graph whose neighbours are up / down / left / right.
signals: Connectivity: *number of islands / provinces / connected components*.
Shortest path in an unweighted graph or grid points to BFS.
Reachability, flood fill, cycle detection, topological order point to DFS.

variations.name: DFS (recursion / stack)
variations.desc: Connected components, flood fill, path existence.
code: void dfs(int u, vector<vector<int>>& g, vector<bool>& seen) {
for (int v : g[u]) if (!seen[v]) dfs(v, g, seen);

variations.name: BFS (queue)
variations.desc: Fewest steps / shortest path in unweighted graphs and grids.

variations.name: Grid traversal
variations.desc: Treat each cell as a node with 4 (or 8) neighbours: `Number of Islands`, `Rotting Oranges`.

variations.name: Topological sort & cycle detection
variations.desc: DFS post-order or Kahn's BFS on a directed acyclic graph (course schedule).

complexity: O(V + E) — every vertex and edge is visited once.
pitfalls: Mark a node visited when you *enqueue* it (BFS), not when you dequeue, or you add it twice.
Deep graphs can blow the recursion stack — switch to an explicit stack if needed.

name: Graphs — Advanced
tagline: Weights and connectivity: the classic algorithms.
core_idea: Once edges carry weights or you need global structure, plain BFS/DFS is not enough — you reach for specialised algorithms: weighted shortest paths (**Dijkstra** / **Bellman-Ford**), minimum spanning trees (**Kruskal** / **Prim**), and dynamic connectivity (**Union-Find**). The skill is recognising which classic algorithm a problem is secretly asking for.
signals: Weighted shortest paths (Dijkstra for non-negative; Bellman-Ford for negative edges).
*Connect all nodes at minimum cost* points to a Minimum Spanning Tree.
Dynamic connectivity, *are these in the same group*, undirected cycle detection point to Union-Find.
All-pairs shortest paths on a small graph point to Floyd-Warshall.

variations.name: Dijkstra (heap)
variations.desc: Shortest path from a source with non-negative weights.
code: if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.push({dist[v], v}); }

variations.name: Union-Find (DSU)
variations.desc: Connected components, redundant connection, the backbone of Kruskal's MST.
code: int find(int x){ return par[x] == x ? x : par[x] = find(par[x]); }
void uni(int a, int b){ par[find(a)] = find(b); }

variations.name: Minimum Spanning Tree
variations.desc: Kruskal (sort edges + DSU) or Prim (grow from a node with a heap).

variations.name: Bellman-Ford / Floyd-Warshall
variations.desc: Negative edges (Bellman-Ford) or all-pairs shortest paths (Floyd-Warshall).

complexity: Dijkstra O((V+E) log V); Union-Find ~O(alpha(n)) per op; Kruskal O(E log E).
pitfalls: Dijkstra breaks with negative edges — use Bellman-Ford there.
Always add path compression + union by rank to Union-Find or it degrades.

name: Backtracking
tagline: Try a choice, recurse, then undo it.
core_idea: Backtracking builds candidate solutions one choice at a time and abandons (*backtracks on*) a path the moment it cannot lead to a valid answer. It is a guided DFS over the tree of all possibilities: **choose to recurse to un-choose**. Pruning invalid branches early is what makes an exponential space tractable.
signals: *Generate all* or *count all* subsets, permutations, combinations.
Constraint puzzles: N-Queens, Sudoku, word search, palindrome partitioning.
You need every solution, not just one optimum (that is usually DP or greedy).

variations.name: Subsets / combinations
variations.desc: At each element, branch on include vs skip.

variations.name: Permutations
variations.desc: Try each unused element at the current position; track a `used[]` array.

variations.name: Constraint search with pruning
variations.desc: N-Queens, Sudoku — kill a branch the instant it becomes invalid.

complexity: Exponential in the worst case (O(2^n) subsets, O(n!) permutations); pruning cuts the real cost dramatically.
pitfalls: Always undo the choice after recursing (restore state) or branches bleed into each other.
Skip duplicates (sort first, then skip equal siblings) to avoid repeated answers.

name: Dynamic Programming
tagline: Solve overlapping subproblems once.
core_idea: DP solves a problem by combining answers to **overlapping subproblems** and storing each answer so it is computed once. If a brute-force recursion keeps re-solving the same smaller cases, add memoization (top-down) or fill a table bottom-up. The hard part is naming the **state** and writing the **recurrence** (transition) between states.
signals: *Number of ways*, *min / max cost or length*, *can we reach / partition* — with choices that overlap.
A recursive solution recomputes the same arguments; results depend only on a few parameters.
Optimal substructure: the best answer is built from best answers to subproblems.

variations.name: 1D DP
variations.desc: `Climbing Stairs`, `House Robber`, `Decode Ways`.
code: for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2];

variations.name: 2D / grid DP
variations.desc: Edit distance, longest common subsequence, unique paths.

variations.name: Knapsack family
variations.desc: 0/1, unbounded, subset-sum, coin change — choose to take an item or not.

variations.name: Interval / subsequence DP
variations.desc: Palindromes, matrix-chain, LIS (also O(n log n) via binary search).

variations.name: Top-down memoization
variations.desc: Recursion plus a cache, when the table shape is awkward to fill iteratively.

complexity: Usually O(states x transitions) time and O(states) space — often reducible to a rolling O(1)/O(n) row.
pitfalls: Define the state precisely and the base cases before coding.
Iterate in an order where every dependency is already computed.

name: Greedy / Intervals
tagline: Locally best choice; sort then sweep.
core_idea: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders — fast and simple, but correct only when a local optimum provably leads to a global one (the *greedy-choice property*). A huge family of greedy problems is about **intervals**: sort by start or end, then sweep once, merging or counting as you go.
signals: *Maximum number of non-overlapping ...*, *minimum number of ... to cover ...*.
Intervals: merge, insert, count overlaps, meeting rooms.
Jump games, gas station, resource assignment where sorting reveals the choice.

variations.name: Sort + sweep intervals
variations.desc: Merge overlapping ranges; sort by start, extend or push.

variations.name: Greedy choice by sorting
variations.desc: Activity selection: pick the earliest finishing time first to fit the most.

variations.name: Greedy scan with an invariant
variations.desc: `Jump Game` (track the farthest reach), `Gas Station` (running tank balance).

complexity: Dominated by the sort: O(n log n); the sweep itself is O(n).
pitfalls: Greedy is easy to get wrong — be ready to justify why the local choice is safe, or fall back to DP.
Sort by the right key: finish time vs start time changes the answer.

name: Bit Manipulation
tagline: Compute with raw bits and XOR.
core_idea: Numbers are just bit patterns, and bitwise operators (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) let you flip, test, and combine those bits in O(1). **XOR** is the star: `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a`, so XORing a whole array cancels every pair and leaves the lone element. A **bitmask** also lets you represent a set of up to ~32 / 64 items as a single integer.
signals: *Single number*, *missing number*, counting set bits, power-of-two checks.
Subsets via bitmask, state compression in DP, fast set operations.
Hints like *without using +/-* or *constant extra space*.

complexity: O(1) per bit operation; bitmask DP is O(2^n * n).
pitfalls: Watch signed shifts and overflow — use unsigned types when in doubt.
Bitwise operators have low precedence — parenthesise generously.

name: Math
tagline: Replace loops with number-theory identities.
core_idea: Some problems are really number theory or combinatorics in disguise; spotting the formula or property beats simulating. Common tools: GCD/LCM (Euclid), prime sieves, modular arithmetic for huge counts, fast exponentiation, and combinatorics. The win is replacing an O(n) or O(n^2) loop with an O(log n) or O(1) identity.
signals: *Count the number of ways* (combinatorics), or *modulo 1e9+7* (avoid overflow).
Primes, divisors, GCD/LCM, digit manipulation, base conversion.
Geometry, overflow-sensitive arithmetic, *compute x^n efficiently*.

name: String Matching
tagline: Find a pattern without restarting on a mismatch.
core_idea: Finding a pattern inside a text naively costs O(n*m) because every mismatch restarts the comparison. Smarter algorithms reuse the work already done: **KMP** precomputes how far to safely jump on a mismatch, **Rabin-Karp** compares rolling hashes, and **Z / Manacher** answer prefix and palindrome queries in linear time.
signals: Substring search, *find all occurrences of a pattern*.
Repeated substrings, longest palindromic substring, anagram / substring counting.
Multiple-pattern search (Aho-Corasick) or prefix-function questions.

variations.name: Z-function / Manacher
variations.desc: Prefix matches (Z) or the longest palindromic substring (Manacher) in O(n).

variations.name: Sliding window + frequency

pitfalls: Off-by-one in the prefix table is the classic KMP bug — test it on `aaaa`.
Rabin-Karp needs a verification step (hash collisions) and a good modulus.

name: Design
tagline: Compose structures to hit each operation's time bound.
core_idea: Design problems ask you to build a class or data structure that supports a set of operations within tight time bounds — the trick is **composing** the right primitive structures so every operation hits its target complexity. Usually it is a hash map paired with one more structure (a linked list, two stacks, a heap) so each method runs in O(1) or O(log n).
signals: *Design X*: LRU cache, min-stack, hash map, trie, rate limiter, iterator.
Strict per-operation complexity requirements (*all operations O(1)*).
Implement-a-data-structure or simulate-a-system prompts.
